newsitem.title: COMOROS: Detained men are not hijackers - Ethiopian pilot.
newsitem.headline: Detained men are not hijackers - Ethiopian pilot.

text.p: The co-pilot of the Ethiopian Airlines plane that crashed near the Comoro Islands was unable to identify two detained men as suspected hijackers, officials said on Tuesday.
The hijacked plane ditched in the sea off the idyllic holiday islands on Saturday after it ran out of fuel some 500 metres (yards) from the beach.
Ethiopian Airlines' coordinator at the crash site, Sultan Mohammed, said the injured co-pilot Yonas Mekuria was taken to see the two men on Monday.
"He did not identify them, yet he knew two of the three hijackers," Sultan told reporters near the site of the crash in which about 125 of the 175 passengers and crew perished.
The two men were identified as suspected hijackers by some of the injured survivors when police took them to the main hospital in the Comoro capital Moroni on Sunday.
Since then the two men, who have not been charged, have been held in custody.
Sultan said the two men had denied any involvement in the hijacking.
Mekuria's nose and some of his fingers were broken by two of the hijackers in a fight before the plane crashed.
The co-pilot, the pilot and other survivors say there were three hijackers.
The pilot of the Boeing 767 has returned to Addis Ababa and other survivors have also left the Indian Ocean islands.
Sultan said Mekuria had looked at some of the bodies in a makeshift morgue in Moroni and had not seen any sign of the hijackers.
Mekuria will have to look at another 27 bodies recovered on Monday and the final 12 which French military firemen hope to cut clear of the wreckage on Tuesday.
The plane was hijacked by the three men, believed to be Ethiopians, when it was en route to Nairobi and West Africa from the Ethiopian capital.
Senior Comoron government officials said Ethiopia had requested the extradition of the two detained men.

"To my knowledge no decision has been taken about releasing the suspects, but we have received an extradition request from the Ethiopian government," Secretary of State (Minister) for Information Assoumani Youssouf told Reuters.
He was responding to rumours the two men might be released on grounds they had been wrongly identified.
"This is a criminal affair and an inquiry is under way. The two suspects have not been charged and it will be up to the judiciary to take any decisions," said gendarmerie commander Ismael Mognidayo.
Of the 163 passengers and 12 crew on board the plane, 145 were international travellers from some 35 countries and 30 were Ethiopians.
At the makeshift morgue, one nurse and an exhausted Ethiopian Airlines doctor laboured to arrange dozens of bodies, injecting them with formol as a form of basic embalming, witnesses said.

American and Israeli officials who came to the Indian Ocean archipelago to identify and retrieve bodies of their citizens began to squabble with Comoron officials over the organisation of the bodies in the morgue.
A Kenyan and an Indian looking for relatives were forced to look through more than 80 body bags.
The witnesses said it appeared the well-meaning but makeshift operation had started to unravel because the Comoro Islands did not have the capacity to deal with such a disaster.
Ethiopian Airlines made preparations on Monday to return the crash victims to Addis Ababa, but their efforts were hindered by a lack of coffins on the islands.
"The problem we have is that we have no coffins in the Comoros. We are a Moslem country. Possibly Ethiopian Airlines may bring some in," Mognidaho told Reuters.
Moslems bury their dead in shrouds instead of coffins.
